explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 4 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. So far in Stage 8 you have practised finding things out, taking topics apart, and judging how strong an argument is. This unit turns the spotlight around. Instead of thinking about the world, you will think about yourself: how you learn, how you work with other people, and how your own views grow and change. That is the skill of Reflection.

Remember the six skills that run through the whole subject:

This unit is about the fourth skill: Reflection. In Stage 8 you go further than simply saying whether you enjoyed a task. You will look honestly at your own strengths and your areas for development, weigh what you gain and what you struggle with when you work in a team, and track exactly how and why your personal perspective on an issue changed as you learned more. These are grown-up habits of mind, and they make every other skill stronger.

Why does reflection matter beyond school? Think about how adults actually get better at what they do. A nurse reviews a difficult shift and changes one habit for next time. A football coach studies a match the team lost to see what they must practise. A shopkeeper notices which decisions worked and which did not, and adjusts. None of them improve by luck. They improve by stopping, thinking honestly about what happened, and choosing one clear thing to do differently. The learner who reflects well now will keep improving for the rest of their life, in any job they choose. That is why this skill is worth your time.
bullets: Research — finding things out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — taking a topic apart to see its causes, effects and connections.
Evaluation — judging how strong an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking honestly about how you learn, how you work with others, and how your views change.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so clearly that others truly understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning the Ehel Academy way, which is self-paced. Three kinds of support work together, and reflection touches all three:

Older versions of this subject leaned heavily on tasks that only worked in a fixed classroom full of learners. In our model, your AI tutor is your everyday partner and your class, and your teacher sessions are where you meet other learners face to face. So when this unit asks you to reflect on teamwork, think about the real times you work with others: in a teacher session, on a family project, or in your community. And treat every 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box as a real conversation, not just a box to read: say your ideas out loud or type them, and let the tutor push your thinking further than working alone ever could.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. Reflection is naturally private and self-paced. You read, think, and write honestly in your own time, with no one marking you. You decide the order and the speed.

Your AI tutor, available every hour of the day. Wherever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a thoughtful study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It asks you questions, plays back what you say, and helps you notice patterns in how you learn, day or night.
Your teacher, about twice a week. Live sessions are where you practise real teamwork with other learners, share a reflection you are proud of, and get guidance on your next target.

explainers.title: Meet Kian, our reflective learner for this unit
explainers.body:
To make every idea concrete, we will follow one Year 8 learner through the whole unit. His name is Kian, and he studies at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Kian has a strong opinion when the unit begins. He thinks phones and screens are mostly bad for young people. His own screen time keeps him up late, he has watched friends scroll instead of talking, and he would happily ban phones for anyone under fifteen if he could. His starting view is simple and firm: screens are harming young people like me, and we would all be better off with far less of them.

Over this unit, two things happen to Kian. First, he researches the issue and hears other people's viewpoints. Second, he works in a small team with other learners on a shared outcome. Both experiences change him. He does not just collect facts; he starts to notice things about himself, such as how quickly he interrupts and how sure he is that he is right. By the end, his view has grown into something more careful and better supported by evidence, and he can explain exactly how and why it changed. Watching Kian reflect will show you how to reflect on your own learning and your own Challenge.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the issue you reflect on
explainers.body:
Like every unit, this one builds around your Challenge: a global issue that also matters right where you live. For Reflection, the best Challenge is one where you can imagine your own view changing as you learn more, because tracking that change is the heart of this unit.

Here are some issues that are global and also very real across the Horn of Africa. Any of these could be your Challenge, and on each one thoughtful people genuinely disagree:

Other learners in Kian's teacher sessions chose their own Challenges. Zara is looking at plastic bags in the market, Tariq at whether young people should leave the countryside for the city, and Grace at school meals. You will see some of them appear in the examples that follow. You do not have to match anyone else. Choose the issue that makes you most curious, or a little bit angry, because those feelings usually mark a Challenge you will care enough to reflect on honestly.

Before you go further, write down what you think about your Challenge right now, in one honest sentence. That sentence is your starting point. At the end of the unit you will compare it with what you think then, and the gap between them is your reflection made visible.
bullets: Screens, phones and young people: helping, harming, or both?
Whether our markets should limit single-use plastic bags
Moving from the countryside into the city: is it worth it? (migration)
Work and training for young people leaving school
Clean air and the growth of traffic in our towns
Wildlife and tourism along the Berbera coast
Healthy food and good school meals
Renewable energy, such as solar power for homes and schools
Clean water and who should pay to bring it closer to families
School rules on uniforms, phones and timings

explainers.title: What is reflection, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think reflection just means saying whether a lesson was fun or boring. Real reflection is far more useful than that. Reflection is thinking honestly about yourself as a learner: how you worked, what you did well, what you found hard, how you contributed to a team, and how and why your views changed. It looks inward, at you and your learning, rather than outward at the world.

Good reflection in Stage 8 usually moves through a cycle you can use after any piece of work:

Notice that none of these steps is about the topic itself. They are all about you. That is what makes reflection different from the other skills, and it is why honesty matters more here than being right.
bullets: Look back honestly at what you did and how you did it.
Name a strength you used and an area for development you noticed.
Think about how you worked with others, and what you contributed.
Ask whether your personal perspective on the issue changed, and why.
Set a clear, specific target for what you will do differently next time.
Record it, so you can look back and see how far you have come.

explainers.title: Reflection is not the same as evaluation
explainers.body:
This is the idea learners find trickiest at Stage 8, so it is worth getting clear. Evaluation and Reflection are both about judging, but they judge different things.

The two skills work together. You might evaluate a team poster and decide the message was unclear. Then you reflect and realise you stayed quiet when you could have suggested a clearer heading, and you set a target to speak up sooner next time. Evaluation judges the poster; reflection considers your part in it and how you will grow. Keeping the two apart stops you from turning honest self-reflection into a simple review of the work, and it is a habit your teacher will look for this year.
bullets: Evaluation looks outward. It judges the quality of things: How strong is this argument? How reliable is this source? How good is our final outcome? Evaluation is about the work.
Reflection looks inward. It considers you: How did I contribute? What did I do well or badly? How did my view change? What will I do differently? Reflection is about the learner.

explainers.title: Keep a reflection journal
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first sub-skill, start the habit that reflective learners rely on most: keep a reflection journal. This is a notebook or a document where you write honestly about your learning as you go. Each time you finish a piece of work, spend five minutes recording what you did, what went well, what was hard, and what you will try next.

A reflection journal earns its place for three reasons. It captures how you felt and thought in the moment, which is easy to forget later. It shows how your skills and your views change over time, which is exactly what this unit asks you to notice. And it gives you real examples to bring to your teacher sessions and to your final self-assessment. Copy the template below into your journal and use it after each task.

rows: Date
What I worked on
What I did well (a strength I used)
What I found hard (an area to develop)
How I worked with others, and what I contributed
How my view on the issue changed, if at all
My target: next time I will ...

explainers.title: Reflection is private, and that is its strength
explainers.body:
One reason reflection works so well in a self-paced model is that it is honest and private. When no one is marking you and no classmate is watching, it is much easier to admit that you rushed, or stayed quiet, or held on to a view for too long. That honesty is not a weakness to hide; it is the very thing that lets you improve.

You choose what to share. Some reflections stay in your journal for your eyes only. Others you bring to your AI tutor to think through, or to a teacher session because you are proud of the progress. Your tutor is a safe place to be honest: it will not judge you, and it will help you turn a hard admission into a clear next step. The braver you are with yourself here, the faster you grow.

explainers.title: Skill 1: Knowing your strengths and your areas for development
explainers.body:
Good reflection starts with an honest map of yourself. A personal strength is something you are good at. An area for development is something you find hard or have not learned yet. Naming both, fairly, is a Stage 8 skill in itself, because it is tempting either to boast or to be too hard on yourself.

In Global Perspectives, useful strengths and areas for development include things like listening to others, asking good questions, researching for evidence, giving reasons for a claim, summarising in your own words, and letting other people take a turn. You will be strong at some and still growing in others, and that is completely normal. Nobody is strong at all of them at once.

explainers.title: Skill 2: Reflecting on your contribution to teamwork
explainers.body:
Cambridge objective 4.1 asks you to explain your personal contribution to teamwork and to identify targets for improvement. In the Ehel Academy model, your teamwork happens in real settings: working with other learners in a teacher session, sharing a task with family, or joining a community effort. Reflecting on what you brought to that team is the skill here.

There is a difference between working in a team and working as a team. You work in a team whenever you are simply placed with others. You work as a team when everyone knows their part and pulls together towards one shared outcome. Good teamwork relies on combining each person's individual strengths, so knowing your own strengths, from Skill 1, matters here too.

explainers.title: Skill 3: Weighing the benefits and challenges of teamwork
explainers.body:
Cambridge objective 4.2 asks you to consider the benefits and the challenges of working with others towards a shared outcome. Honest reflection sees both. Teamwork is not simply good or bad; it brings real gains and real difficulties, and a reflective learner can name each without pretending.

The reflective move is not to pretend the challenges do not exist. It is to notice them and think about how to overcome them. Most teamwork challenges are eased by the same habits: listening carefully, being willing to compromise, and making sure everyone knows their job before you start.
bullets: Benefits often include: more ideas than one person could have, shared work, different strengths combined, and encouragement when a task is hard.
Challenges often include: disagreement, uneven effort, people talking over each other, and the time it takes to agree on anything.

explainers.title: Skill 4: Naming the skills you used or improved
explainers.body:
Cambridge objective 4.4 asks you to identify skills you learnt or improved during an activity, and to relate them to your personal strengths and areas for improvement. Every task grows some skill in you, but the growth only counts if you notice it. Reflection is how you notice.

After a piece of work, ask yourself three questions: Which skill did I use most? Did I get better at it, and how can I tell? Is this skill becoming one of my personal strengths, or is it still an area I need to develop? Answering honestly turns a finished task into real, lasting improvement instead of a one-off.

explainers.title: Skill 5: Setting clear, SMART improvement targets
explainers.body: Reflection is only useful if it changes what you do next. That is why every Cambridge reflection objective ends with the same idea: identify a target for improvement. A weak target is vague, like I will do better. A strong target is one you could actually check. A useful way to build a strong target is to make it SMART:
bullets: Specific — it names exactly what you will do, not just do better.
Measurable — you could tell whether you managed it.
Achievable — it is something you can really do.
Realistic — it fits the time and resources you have.
Time-bound — it has a when, such as by my next teacher session.

explainers.title: Skill 6: Tracking how and why your personal perspective changed
explainers.body:
This is the heart of Stage 8 reflection. Cambridge objective 4.3 asks you to consider how your personal perspective on an issue may have changed as a result of research or hearing different perspectives. A personal perspective is the view you hold on an issue after exploring different viewpoints and thinking about the causes and consequences. It is not a random opinion; it is a considered view you can support with evidence.

It helps to tell three kinds of perspective apart:

Your personal perspective can and should develop as you learn. Changing your mind because of good evidence is not weakness; it is exactly what a thoughtful person does. The reflective skill is to notice the change and explain why it happened, always supporting your view with a reason: I think this, because ...
bullets: Personal perspective — the view you hold, shaped by your own research and the viewpoints you have heard.
National perspective — the view a country takes, often shown in its laws, policies and the speeches of its leaders.
Global perspective — a view that takes account of how an issue affects the wider world, across many countries.

explainers.title: Kian's reflection journey, from start to finish
explainers.body: You have now met every reflection sub-skill. Here is how they came together for Kian across the unit, so you can see the whole picture before you try it yourself.

explainers.title: How reflection strengthens the other five skills
explainers.body:
Reflection may look inward, but it improves everything you do outward. Once you can reflect honestly, every other Global Perspectives skill gets sharper, because you keep spotting exactly what to fix.

So the honesty you practise here is never wasted. Reflection is the skill that keeps all the others growing, long after this unit ends. It is the quiet engine behind every learner who keeps getting better year after year.
bullets: Research improves when you notice which methods worked for you and which wasted your time.
Analysis improves when you spot the thinking habits that trip you up, such as jumping to a cause too fast.
Evaluation improves when you can judge your own work as fairly as you judge a source.
Collaboration improves the most, because reflecting on teamwork tells you exactly what to do better next time.
Communication improves when you notice which of your explanations others actually understood.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the reflection cycle
explainers.body:
Here is the whole cycle in one place. You can use it after any task, in any subject, for the rest of your life.

The learners who improve fastest are not the ones who never struggle. They are the ones who stop, reflect honestly, and set a clear target every single time. That habit is now yours to keep.
bullets: Look back honestly at what you did and how you did it.
Name a strength you used and an area for development.
Reflect on how you worked with others and what you contributed.
Ask whether your personal perspective changed, and explain why.
Set one or two clear, SMART targets for next time.
Record it all in your reflection journal, and look back later to see your progress.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Collaboration. Reflection and collaboration are close partners: this unit taught you to reflect on how you work with others, and the next one teaches you to do it well from the start, sharing roles, listening, and building a shared outcome as a real team. The honest self-knowledge you have built here, your strengths, your areas for development, and your targets, will make you a much stronger team member. Well done for having the courage to look inward and to name, clearly, how you want to grow.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to hold on to
lines: Reflection is not about deciding whether you are good or bad. It is about noticing, honestly, how you learn and how you change.
An area you have not mastered yet is not a failure. It is simply your next target, and naming it is the first step to improving.
The most useful sentence in this whole unit is short: next time, I will ...

bigIdeas.title: A quick test to tell them apart
lines: If the sentence is about the argument, the source, or the outcome, it is evaluation.
If the sentence is about you: your effort, your contribution, your skills, or your changing view, it is reflection.
Evaluation asks how good is it? Reflection asks how did I do, and how did I change?

bigIdeas.title: What reflective learners do
lines: They welcome feedback, and they take both praise and criticism calmly, as useful information.
They notice how they learn best: alone, with the AI tutor, or with others in a session.
They can name their own strengths and areas for development, and explain them to someone else.
They do not just spot a weakness; they say clearly how they will improve it.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to many perspectives
lines: On most issues, thoughtful people hold different views for honest reasons, and a reflective learner listens to all of them before deciding.

For example, on whether a school day should pause for a festival, a family who celebrates Eid and a family who celebrates Christmas may each hold a fair view, and hearing both makes your own perspective richer.
Being fair does not mean having no view. It means forming your view only after you have listened honestly to others.

bigIdeas.title: Turning feedback into a target
lines: Thank the person, then repeat the point back in your own words to check you understood it.
Ask yourself: is this feedback fair? Often part of it is, even if not all.
Turn the fair part into one specific target, and write it in your journal.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one global issue that also matters where you live, ideally one where you can imagine your own view changing.
You will reflect on it again and again, so choose something you genuinely have feelings about.
By the end you will be able to explain, with evidence, how your view grew.

bigIdeas.title: Give evidence, not just a feeling
lines: Do not only write I am good at research. Add the proof: because last unit I cross-checked three sources.
Evidence stops you overrating or underrating yourself.
It also gives you a real example to bring to your teacher session.

bigIdeas.title: Working in a team versus as a team
lines: You work in a team when you are simply placed with others.
You work as a team when everyone knows their part and pulls towards one shared outcome.
Strong teamwork combines each person's individual strengths, so knowing your own matters.

bigIdeas.title: Challenges are not reasons to avoid teamwork
lines: Every team meets challenges; a good team expects them and plans for them.
The reflective question is not was it hard? but how did we handle the hard part?
Naming a challenge honestly is the first step to overcoming it next time.

bigIdeas.title: There is no single best way to learn
lines: Some learners think best alone, some when talking to the AI tutor, some in a live session.
The same learner may prefer different supports for different tasks.
Noticing which works for you, and when, is one of the most useful things you can learn this year.

bigIdeas.title: What a strong reflection needs
lines: It is about the learner, not only the task.
It is honest and specific, not vague.
It gives evidence or a reason.
It ends with a clear target where that fits.

models.title: Reflection happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine you helped cook a family meal and the rice came out undercooked.
You look back honestly: you turned off the heat too early because you were rushing.
You name a strength: you seasoned it well. And an area to develop: you need to check the timing, not guess.
You set a target: next time I will use a timer and taste before serving.
That is reflection, and you already do it whenever you decide to do something better next time.

models.title: Kian's example: an honest self-map
lines: Strengths: Kian is good at researching for evidence and at organising information into a clear order.
Areas for development: he interrupts when he is excited, and he finds it hard to let quieter people speak.
He explains why: he loves being right, which helps his research but hurts his listening.
Naming this honestly is not a criticism of Kian. It is the first step to a target he can actually work on.

The trick is to give evidence for what you claim, just as you would for any argument. Do not only say I am good at research. Say I am good at research, because last unit I found three sources and cross-checked them. Evidence turns a vague feeling into a reflection you can trust and build on, and it stops you either overrating or underrating yourself.

models.title: Kian's example: his part in a shared outcome
lines: In two teacher sessions, Kian worked with Leila, Omar and Nadia to build a short awareness poster about healthy screen habits for younger students.
His contribution: he gathered the research and organised the facts into a clear order, which he is good at.
His honest weakness: he took over the wording and did not ask Nadia, the quietest, for her ideas.
His target: next time I will ask each person for one idea before I start writing, so every strength is used.

Notice that Kian does not just say I helped a lot. He says exactly what he did, links it to a strength, admits one honest weakness, and sets a specific target. That is what a Stage 8 reflection on teamwork looks like: precise, honest, and pointed at what happens next.

models.title: Kian's example: the good and the hard
lines: A benefit Kian felt: Leila suggested an idea about family businesses that he would never have thought of alone, which made the poster stronger.
A challenge Kian felt: he and Omar disagreed about the main message, and the team lost time arguing.
How they overcame it: their teacher, Mr Diallo, suggested they each explain their reason, then choose. They compromised on a message that used both ideas.
Kian's reflection: teamwork gave us richer ideas but cost us time; next time I will listen for the point behind a disagreement sooner.

models.title: Kian's example: spotting the skill that grew
lines: The skill Kian used most: summarising research in his own words for the poster.
How he knows he improved: his first summary was long and copied; his third was short, clear and truly his own.
The link to his strengths: summarising is becoming a strength, built on his existing strength in organising.
The area still to develop: listening, which the poster did not push him to practise, so it stays on his target list.

Notice that Kian relates each skill back to his self-map from Skill 1. That is what 'relate to personal strengths and areas for improvement' means: you connect what you did today to the bigger picture of who you are becoming as a learner. Over a year, those small noticings add up to real change.

models.title: Kian's example: weak target versus SMART target
lines: Weak target: I will be a better team member.
SMART target: in my next teacher session, I will ask each team member for one idea before I start writing.
It is specific, you could measure whether he did it, it is achievable and realistic, and it has a clear time.
Because the target is clear, Kian can actually work on it and check it off afterwards.

Aim to set just one or two targets at a time. Two targets you truly act on are worth far more than ten you forget. Write your targets in your reflection journal, and check them at your next teacher session. Meeting a target is a real achievement, and it is a great thing to reflect on in turn.

models.title: Kian's example: a perspective that developed
lines: Before: Kian thought screens are mostly harmful, and young people would be better off with far fewer.

What changed him: a health article showed late-night screens harm sleep, which fitted his view, but Leila explained she runs her family shop's online orders on a phone, and Omar learns English from videos.
After: Kian now thinks screens can help or harm, and the real question is which uses and how much, not simply banning them.
His evidence: the sleep research, Leila's business, and Omar's learning together support this more careful view.

Kian's perspective did not flip to the opposite. It grew into something more careful and better supported. Sometimes your view will change a lot; sometimes it will stay the same but become stronger because you found evidence for it. Both are real reflection, as long as you can say why. What you must avoid is letting your view drift without noticing, or refusing to move even when the evidence clearly points the other way.

models.title: Kian's journey in one place
lines: Skill 1: He mapped his strengths (research, organising) and areas to develop (interrupting, not listening).
Skill 2: He explained his real contribution to the team poster, and set a target about asking others first.
Skill 3: He weighed the benefits (richer ideas) and challenges (lost time) of teamwork honestly.
Skill 4: He noticed that summarising became a strength, while listening stayed an area to develop.
Skill 5: He set a SMART target he could actually check by his next teacher session.
Skill 6: He tracked how his perspective on screens grew from ban them into a careful, evidence-based view.

By reflecting, Kian did not just finish some tasks. He became a clearer thinker who knows his own strengths, works better with others, and can explain why he believes what he believes. In the Activities file you will make the same journey with your own Challenge, one honest step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.

models.title: A model: Zara's contribution
lines: Shared outcome: a market survey about plastic bags, done with two other learners in a teacher session.
Zara's contribution: she wrote the survey questions clearly, which is a strength of hers.
What she could improve: she rushed the others and did not check they agreed with the questions.
Her target: next time, I will read each question aloud and ask the team if it is fair before we use it.

models.title: A model: Omar's improved skill
lines: Skill used most: giving reasons for a claim, when he explained why videos help him learn English.
How he can tell he improved: at first he just said videos are useful; later he gave a clear reason and an example.
Becoming a strength or still developing: becoming a strength, he thinks.
A skill he did not practise: summarising, which he still wants to grow.

models.title: A model: how a view can develop
lines: Before: single-use plastic bags should simply be banned everywhere.
After: bags should be reduced, but only if market sellers get an affordable alternative first, because a seller Zara spoke to would lose customers overnight.
This view did not flip; it grew more careful, and it is now supported by a real viewpoint.
The change came from one honest conversation, not from being told what to think.

models.title: A model: turning a weakness into a SMART target
lines: Weakness noticed: I give up when a source is hard to read.
Weak target: I will read harder sources.
SMART target: this week, I will finish one difficult source by asking my AI tutor to explain any paragraph I get stuck on.
It is specific, checkable, achievable, realistic, and has a clear time.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 4 of Stage 8 Global Perspectives, and the skill is Reflection.
Ask it: What is the difference between reflecting on my learning and simply saying whether I enjoyed a lesson?
Then tell the tutor one thing you already think you are good at, and one thing you would like to get better at this year.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think reflection means at Stage 8.
Ask it: How is reflecting on my learning different from evaluating whether a source is reliable?
Then describe one small thing you did this week, and let the tutor walk you through the reflection cycle on it.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor two sentences: one that evaluates something, and one that reflects on yourself.
Ask it to tell you which is which, and to explain any it thinks you mixed up.
Ask the tutor for one more example of each, using your own Challenge topic.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor two personal strengths and two areas you want to develop, with one piece of evidence for each.
Ask it: Am I being fair to myself, or too hard, or too easy?
Ask the tutor to help you turn one area for development into a clear target you could actually work on.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe to your AI tutor one real time you worked with others, in a teacher session, at home, or in your community.
Say exactly what you contributed, and name one thing you could have done better.
Ask the tutor to help you turn that weakness into one clear target for your next piece of teamwork.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one clear benefit and one clear challenge you have felt when working with others.
Ask it to suggest two practical ways to overcome that challenge next time.
Ask the tutor: on balance, when is teamwork worth the extra effort, and when might working alone be better?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the last piece of Global Perspectives work you did, and the one skill you used most.
Ask it to help you decide whether you improved that skill, and how you could prove it.
Ask the tutor whether that skill is becoming a strength for you, or is still an area to develop.

toolkit.title: Why reflect at all?
toolkit.intro: Reflection is the skill that keeps all the others growing. Research, analysis, evaluation, collaboration and communication each get better when you stop and notice, honestly, how you did and what you would change. Without reflection, you can repeat the same mistake for years without seeing it. With it, every task becomes a chance to improve. That is why Stage 8 treats reflection as a serious skill, not an afterthought.

toolkit.title: A one-minute reflection for busy days
toolkit.intro:
Reflection does not have to be long to be useful. On a day when you have almost no time, a single honest line still counts, as long as it is about you and points forward. Try this quick version after any task.

Three short lines like these, written often, add up to far more growth over a year than one long reflection you never quite get around to writing. When you have more time, use the fuller templates below.
items: One thing that went well was ...
One thing I would change is ...
So next time, I will ...

toolkit.title: The reflection cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever the task, good reflection follows the same steps. Come back to this list whenever you finish a piece of work.
items: Look back: honestly review what you did and how you did it.
Name: a strength you used and an area for development.
Teamwork: reflect on how you worked with others and what you contributed.
Perspective: ask whether your view changed, and explain why.
Target: set one or two clear, SMART targets for next time.
Record: write it in your reflection journal and look back later.

toolkit.title: The Reflection skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Reflection is thinking honestly about yourself as a learner: how you worked, what you did well, what you found hard, how you contributed to a team, and how and why your views changed. It looks inward, at you, rather than outward at the world.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, be honest, because reflection only helps if you tell yourself the truth, even when it is uncomfortable. Second, always finish with a target, because reflection is only useful if it changes what you do next. If you remember nothing else from this unit, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Reflection versus evaluation
toolkit.intro: These two skills are easy to mix up, so keep this contrast handy. A quick test: if the sentence is about the work, it is evaluation; if it is about you, it is reflection.

rows: Reflection
Looks inward, at you and your learning.
How did I contribute? How did my view change? What will I do next?
Evaluation
Looks outward, at the quality of the work.
How strong is this argument? How reliable is this source? How good is our outcome?

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 8 Reflection objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong reflection looks like at this stage. Here are the official Reflection objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Explain personal contribution to teamwork and identify targets for improvement.
Say clearly what you added to a team, and set a target to do it even better.
Consider the benefits and challenges of teamwork experienced when working together to achieve a shared outcome.
Weigh honestly what you gained and what you struggled with when working with others.
Consider ways that personal perspective on an issue may have changed as a result of conducting research or exploring different perspectives.
Notice how and why your own view grew or changed as you learned more, and support it with evidence.
Identify skills learnt or improved during an activity and relate to personal strengths and areas for improvement.
Spot the skills a task grew in you, and link them to who you are becoming as a learner.

toolkit.title: Template: Your reflection journal
toolkit.intro: Copy this table into your journal and fill it in after each piece of work. Keep entries short and honest; five minutes is enough.

rows: Date
What I worked on
A strength I used
An area I found hard
How I worked with others
How my view changed, if at all
My target: next time I will ...

toolkit.title: Template: Before-and-after viewpoint
toolkit.intro: Use this frame to track how your personal perspective on an issue develops over a unit.

rows: My issue (as a question)
Before, I thought ...
What I researched or heard that affected me
Now, I think ... because ...
Did my view change a lot, a little, or stay the same but stronger?

toolkit.title: Template: Setting a SMART target
toolkit.intro: A strong target is one you could actually check. Test each target against these five letters before you commit to it.

rows: Specific
Does it name exactly what I will do?
Measurable
Could I tell whether I managed it?
Achievable
Is it something I can really do?
Realistic
Does it fit my time and resources?
Time-bound
Does it have a clear when, such as by my next teacher session?

toolkit.title: Template: Reflecting on teamwork
toolkit.intro: Use this frame after any task you did with other people, in a session, at home, or in your community.

rows: The shared outcome we worked towards
What I personally contributed
A benefit of working as a team
A challenge, and how we could overcome it
My target for better teamwork next time

toolkit.title: How to reflect after a teacher session
toolkit.intro: Teacher sessions are where you do your real teamwork, so they are worth a short reflection each time. Straight after a session, spend a few minutes on these steps.
items: Note the one idea from the session that most made you think.
Write what you contributed, and one thing you would do differently.
Note any viewpoint you heard that was different from your own.
Add one line to your reflection journal, and carry any target to your next session.

toolkit.title: Taking praise and criticism well
toolkit.intro: Reflective learners welcome feedback, and they take both praise and criticism calmly, as useful information rather than as a judgement of who they are. When someone praises your work, notice exactly what worked so you can do it again. When someone points out a problem, resist the urge to defend yourself; instead, ask what one change would help most. Feedback from your AI tutor, your teacher, and the people you work with is one of the fastest ways to improve, but only if you are willing to hear it.

toolkit.title: Personal, national and global perspectives
toolkit.intro: Telling these three apart helps you reflect clearly on whose view you are describing.

rows: Personal perspective
The view you hold after exploring viewpoints and reasons.
I think screens can help or harm, depending on how they are used.
National perspective
The view a country takes, shown in its laws and leaders' speeches.
A country passes a law limiting phone use in schools.
Global perspective
A view that takes account of how an issue affects the wider world.
Screen habits affect young people's health across many countries.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for reflection
toolkit.intro: Use these to write clear, honest reflections. Say what you mean, and give a reason.

toolkit.title: About your strengths and skills
items: One thing I did well was ..., because ...
One thing I found hard was ...
The skill I most improved was ..., and I can tell because ...

toolkit.title: About teamwork
items: My contribution to the team was ...
A benefit of teamwork was ..., but a challenge was ...
Next time I work in a team, I will ...

toolkit.title: About your changing perspective
items: At the start I thought ..., but now I think ..., because ...
My view stayed the same but grew stronger, because ...
The viewpoint that most changed my thinking was ...

toolkit.title: About your next target
items: My target for next time is ..., and I will check it by ...

challenge.intro: Objective 4.2 asks you to see both sides of teamwork honestly. Using the same team experience, or another one, weigh what you gained against what you found difficult. A good reflection here refuses to pretend teamwork is all easy or all hard.
topics: Write one real benefit you felt from working with others.
Write one real challenge you faced.
Write one practical way that challenge could be overcome next time.
Finish this sentence honestly: for this kind of task, teamwork was worth it, or not worth it, because ...
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Capture your starting perspective
activities.label: Activity 1: Capture your starting perspective
activities.intro: Reflection needs a starting point to measure from. Before you learn anything new this unit, write down honestly what you think about your Challenge right now. Do not try to sound clever or balanced; just say what you actually believe today. A rough, honest sentence is far more useful here than a polished one, because its whole job is to be compared with what you think later.
steps: Write your Challenge as a question, such as: Are screens helping or harming young people?
Complete this sentence honestly: Right now, I think ... because ...
Write one reason someone might disagree with you, even if you do not agree with them.
Rate how sure you feel, from 1 (not sure at all) to 5 (completely sure).
Date this entry and keep it safe. This is your 'before' snapshot.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your starting perspective to your AI tutor, including your reason and how sure you feel.
Ask it: Is my view supported by a reason, or is it just a feeling right now?
Ask the tutor to describe one thoughtful person who would disagree with me, and why they might.

activities.title: Map your strengths and areas for development
activities.label: Activity 2: Map your strengths and areas for development
activities.intro: An honest self-map is the foundation of reflection, and it feeds every other activity in this unit. Look at the list of learning skills below and decide, for each, whether it is a strength, an area for development, or somewhere in between. Try to be fair rather than modest or boastful.
steps: Listening carefully to the ideas of others
Asking clear questions
Researching for evidence
Giving reasons for a claim
Summarising information in my own words
Letting other people take their turn
Staying calm when someone disagrees with me
Choose two you think are your strengths, and write one piece of evidence for each.
Choose two you want to develop, and write why you think each is hard for you.
For one area for development, write a first idea for how you could improve it.

boxes.title: Give evidence, not just a feeling
lines: Do not only write I am good at research. Add the proof: because last unit I cross-checked three sources.
Evidence stops you overrating or underrating yourself.
It also gives you a real example to bring to your teacher session.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your two strengths and two areas for development to your AI tutor, with your evidence.
Ask it: Am I being fair to myself, or too hard, or too easy?
Ask the tutor to help you turn one area for development into a clear, specific target.

boxes.title: Ask someone who knows you
lines: Ask a family member or your teacher what they think one of your strengths is.
Compare their answer with your own self-map, and notice anything that surprises you.
A strength others see that you missed is worth adding to your list.

activities.title: Reflect on your contribution to a team
activities.label: Activity 3: Reflect on your contribution to a team
activities.intro: Objective 4.1 is about explaining your personal contribution to teamwork. Think of one real time you worked with others: a teacher session, a family task, or a community activity. Reflect honestly on what you brought to it, not what the team did as a whole.
steps: Describe the shared outcome the team was working towards, in one sentence.
Write exactly what you contributed, and link it to one of your strengths.
Write one thing you could have done better as a team member.
Turn that into a target that starts: next time, I will ...

boxes.title: Working in a team versus as a team
lines: You work in a team when you are simply placed with others.
You work as a team when everyone knows their part and pulls towards one shared outcome.
Strong teamwork combines each person's individual strengths, so knowing your own matters.

boxes.title: A model: Zara's contribution
lines: Shared outcome: a market survey about plastic bags, done with two other learners in a teacher session.
Zara's contribution: she wrote the survey questions clearly, which is a strength of hers.
What she could improve: she rushed the others and did not check they agreed with the questions.
Her target: next time, I will read each question aloud and ask the team if it is fair before we use it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about your team experience and exactly what you contributed.
Ask it whether your contribution was clear, and where you could have added more.
Ask the tutor to check that your target is specific enough to act on.

activities.title: Notice the skills you used or improved
activities.label: Activity 5: Notice the skills you used or improved
activities.intro: Objective 4.4 is about spotting the skills a task grew in you. Look back at the work you have done in this unit or a recent one. A skill only counts as improved if you can show how you can tell.
steps: Name the one skill you used the most.
Decide whether you improved it, and write how you can tell.
Say whether that skill is becoming a personal strength, or is still an area to develop.
Name one skill the task did not give you a chance to practise, that you still want to grow.

boxes.title: A model: Omar's improved skill
lines: Skill used most: giving reasons for a claim, when he explained why videos help him learn English.
How he can tell he improved: at first he just said videos are useful; later he gave a clear reason and an example.
Becoming a strength or still developing: becoming a strength, he thinks.
A skill he did not practise: summarising, which he still wants to grow.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the skill you used most and your evidence that it improved.
Ask it to help you decide if that skill is now a strength or still developing.
Ask the tutor to suggest a task that would let you practise the skill you have not grown yet.

activities.title: Before and after - has your view changed?
activities.label: Activity 6: Before and after - has your view changed?
activities.intro: This is the most important activity in the unit. Go back to the starting perspective you wrote in Activity 1. Now that you have researched and heard other viewpoints, look honestly at whether your personal perspective has changed. Remember that a view can change a lot, change a little, or stay the same but grow stronger, and all three are real reflection.
steps: Read your 'before' sentence from Activity 1 again.
Write what you think now: Now, I think ... because ...
Decide which is true for you: my view changed a lot, my view changed a little, or my view stayed the same but is now stronger.
Write the one piece of research or the one viewpoint that most affected your thinking, and why.
Rate how sure you feel now, from 1 to 5, and compare it with your rating in Activity 1.

boxes.title: A model: how a view can develop
lines: Before: single-use plastic bags should simply be banned everywhere.
After: bags should be reduced, but only if market sellers get an affordable alternative first, because a seller Zara spoke to would lose customers overnight.
This view did not flip; it grew more careful, and it is now supported by a real viewpoint.
The change came from one honest conversation, not from being told what to think.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your before and after sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you explain clearly why your view changed, or why it grew stronger.
Ask the tutor whether your new view is supported by evidence, and where it could be stronger.

activities.title: What helped me learn?
activities.label: Activity 7: What helped me learn?
activities.intro: Reflective learners notice how they learn best, not only what they learned. In the Ehel Academy model you learn in several ways, and different ways suit different tasks. Think back across this unit and weigh up each kind of support.
steps: Working on my own, at my own pace, helped my learning a lot / a little / not much, because ...
Working with my AI tutor helped a lot / a little / not much, because ...
Working with other learners and my teacher in sessions helped a lot / a little / not much, because ...
Asking a family member or someone in my community helped a lot / a little / not much, because ...
Now write one sentence: I seem to learn best when ...

boxes.title: There is no single best way to learn
lines: Some learners think best alone, some when talking to the AI tutor, some in a live session.
The same learner may prefer different supports for different tasks.
Noticing which works for you, and when, is one of the most useful things you can learn this year.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which kind of support helped your learning most this unit, and why.
Ask it whether your answer might change for a different kind of task, such as research versus reflection.
Ask the tutor for one way to get more out of the support you use least.

activities.title: Reflect on the process itself
activities.label: Activity 8: Reflect on the process itself
activities.intro: Sometimes the most useful reflection is about how the work went, not just the result. Look back at the whole process of researching your Challenge and working with others, and reflect on the process itself.
steps: What part of the process went smoothly, and why do you think it did?
Where did the process get stuck, slow, or messy?
If you started the same Challenge again tomorrow, what one thing would you do differently from the start?
What did this process teach you about how you like to work?

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe to your AI tutor how the process of this unit actually went for you, the smooth parts and the messy parts.
Ask it to help you name the single biggest change that would have made the process easier.
Ask the tutor to turn that into a habit you could carry into the next unit.

activities.title: Set your improvement targets
activities.label: Activity 9: Set your improvement targets
activities.intro: Reflection only counts if it changes what you do next. Turn what you have noticed across these activities into one or two clear targets you will actually act on. Make each one SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
steps: Choose one area for development you most want to work on.
Draft a target for it, then check it against all five SMART letters and improve it.
Write when you will check whether you met it, such as by my next teacher session.
Optional: set a second SMART target, but no more than two in total.

boxes.title: A model: turning a weakness into a SMART target
lines: Weakness noticed: I give up when a source is hard to read.
Weak target: I will read harder sources.
SMART target: this week, I will finish one difficult source by asking my AI tutor to explain any paragraph I get stuck on.
It is specific, checkable, achievable, realistic, and has a clear time.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your target to your AI tutor and ask which SMART letters it already meets.
Ask it to help you rewrite any part that is vague.
Ask the tutor to suggest how you could prove, next week, that you met the target.

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your one or two SMART targets.
Share them in your next teacher session and ask your teacher to check in on them next time.

practice.intro: Answer these in your journal or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files, and try every one before checking the key. If some feel tricky, that is how you find out what to revisit.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does reflection mean in Global Perspectives?
practice.answer: Reflection means thinking honestly about yourself as a learner: how you worked, what you did well or found hard, how you contributed to others, and how your views changed. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: What is the main difference between reflection and evaluation?
practice.answer: Reflection looks inward at you and your learning; evaluation looks outward at the quality of the work, such as an argument, a source, or an outcome.

practice.prompt: A thing you are good at is a personal ______; a thing you find hard is an area for ______.
practice.answer: Strength; development (an area for development or improvement).

practice.prompt: True or false: changing your mind because of good evidence is a weakness.
practice.answer: False. Changing your mind because of good evidence is thoughtful, not weak.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between working in a team and working as a team?
practice.answer: You work in a team when you are simply placed with others; you work as a team when everyone knows their part and pulls towards one shared outcome.

practice.prompt: Name one benefit and one challenge of teamwork.
practice.answer: Any one benefit (more ideas, shared work, combined strengths, encouragement) and any one challenge (disagreement, uneven effort, talking over each other, time taken).

practice.prompt: Name one habit that helps a team overcome its challenges.
practice.answer: Any one of: listening carefully, being willing to compromise, making sure everyone knows their job.

practice.prompt: A ______ perspective is the view you hold after exploring different viewpoints and reasons.
practice.answer: Personal perspective.

practice.prompt: Which perspective is shown in a country's laws, policies and leaders' speeches: personal, national, or global?
practice.answer: National perspective.

practice.prompt: What does each letter of a SMART target stand for?
practice.answer: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound.

practice.prompt: Rewrite this weak target to make it stronger: 'I will be better at teamwork.'
practice.answer: Any specific, checkable version, such as: in my next teacher session, I will ask each team member for one idea before I start writing.

practice.prompt: When you state your personal perspective, what short phrase should follow it to give a reason?
practice.answer: 'because ...' (as in 'I think this, because ...'), giving a reason for your view.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why keeping a reflection journal is useful.
practice.answer: Any one of: it captures what you thought in the moment; it shows how your skills and views change over time; it gives you real examples for self-assessment.

practice.prompt: True or false: a view that stays the same but becomes stronger is not real reflection.
practice.answer: False. A view that stays the same but becomes stronger, because you found evidence for it, is real reflection.

practice.prompt: Name one skill you can relate to your personal strengths and areas for improvement.
practice.answer: Any learning skill, such as researching, summarising, listening, or giving reasons for a claim.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each reflection word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Reflection
options: A. Something you find hard or have not learned yet.
B. Working with others, combining strengths towards a shared outcome.
C. Thinking honestly about how you learn, work with others, and change.
D. A clear, specific thing you will do to improve next time.
E. Something you are good at.
F. The view you hold on an issue after exploring viewpoints and reasons.
practice.answer: C — Thinking honestly about how you learn, work with others, and change.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Personal strength
practice.answer: E — Something you are good at.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Area for development
practice.answer: A — Something you find hard or have not learned yet.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Personal perspective
practice.answer: F — The view you hold on an issue after exploring viewpoints and reasons.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Target
practice.answer: D — A clear, specific thing you will do to improve next time.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Teamwork
practice.answer: B — Working with others, combining strengths towards a shared outcome.

practice.intro: Look back at your ticks above. Choose two goals you most want to improve, and set a SMART target for each. A good target is specific and has a clear 'when', such as: 'In my next teacher session, I will ask a quieter team member for their idea before I give mine.'
practice.prompt: Area to improve: ______. My SMART target: ______.
Area to improve: ______. My SMART target: ______.

reflection.prompt: This source is out of date, so it is not reliable.
I stayed quiet in the team when I should have shared my idea.
reflection.modelAnswer: R - it is about the learner's own action.

reflection.prompt: Our poster's main message was unclear.
I got much better at summarising in my own words this unit.
reflection.modelAnswer: R - it is about the learner improving.

reflection.prompt: The argument is weak because it gives no evidence.
My view on screens changed after I heard Leila's story.
reflection.modelAnswer: R - it is about the learner's changing view.
'The lesson was fun' is about enjoyment, not learning. Stronger: I enjoyed the lesson because researching in my own words is becoming a strength.

reflection.prompt: I was good in my team.
reflection.modelAnswer: 'I was good in my team' is vague, with no evidence. Stronger: I helped my team by organising our facts clearly, but I need to ask quieter members for their ideas.

reflection.prompt: I will do better next time.
reflection.modelAnswer: 'I will do better next time' is not specific. Stronger: next time, I will read each survey question aloud to check it is fair before we use it.
'My view did not change' gives no reason. Stronger: my view stayed the same but grew stronger, because I found evidence that supported it.

reflection.prompt: Tariq finished a team task but cannot say what he personally added. What one question should he ask himself?
reflection.modelAnswer: He should ask: what did I personally do that the team needed? This names his contribution rather than the team's.

reflection.prompt: Grace says, 'I am bad at everything in teams.' Why is this a weak reflection, and how could she make it fair and useful?
reflection.modelAnswer: It is too harsh and too vague, with no evidence. A fair version names one real strength and one specific area to develop.

reflection.prompt: Kian's view on screens grew more careful after hearing Leila. Is that a weakness or good reflection, and why?
reflection.modelAnswer: Good reflection. Changing your view because of evidence and a new viewpoint is exactly what a thoughtful learner does.

reflection.prompt: Nadia sets the target 'I will listen more.' How could she make it SMART?
reflection.modelAnswer: She could make it SMART, for example: in my next session, I will ask one team member a question and let them finish before I reply.

reflection.prompt: A learner judges that a source is biased. Is that reflection or evaluation, and what would the reflection version sound like?
reflection.modelAnswer: Evaluation, because it judges the source. The reflection version would be about her: for example, I noticed I trusted the source too quickly before checking it.

reflection.prompt: After a team task, Idris only writes 'it went well'. What two things would turn this into a real reflection?
reflection.modelAnswer: He should add what he personally contributed and one specific thing he would do differently next time; a real reflection is about him and points to a next step.

vocabulary.meaning: Thinking honestly about how you learn, work with others, and change.
Judging how strong or good something is, such as an argument, source or outcome.
Something you are good at.
Something you find hard or have not learned yet; an area for improvement.
Working with others, combining strengths, towards a shared outcome.
The single result a team is working together to produce.
What you personally add to a team's work.
A gain or advantage, such as a benefit of working as a team.
A difficulty, such as a challenge of working as a team.
The view you hold on an issue after exploring viewpoints and reasons.
The view a country takes on an issue, shown in laws and leaders' speeches.
A view that takes account of how an issue affects the wider world.
Facts or experience that support a view or a claim.
A clear, specific thing you will do to improve next time.
A target that is specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.
A notebook or file where you record honest reflections as you go.
Helpful comments on your work, which reflective learners welcome.
Judging your own progress honestly against your learning goals.
The things you are good at and the things you still need to develop.
Agreeing to give up part of what you want so a team can move forward.
Getting better at a skill over time, which reflection helps you notice.
Telling yourself the truth in a reflection, even when it is uncomfortable.
The specific part you personally played in a shared piece of work.
Learning in your own time and order, which makes honest, private reflection easier.

mistakes: Saying only whether a task was fun, instead of what you learned about yourself.
Being too hard on yourself, or too easy, instead of fair and honest.
Claiming a strength with no evidence to back it up.
Confusing evaluation (judging the work) with reflection (considering yourself).
Noticing a weakness but setting no target to improve it.
Setting a vague target like 'do better' instead of a specific, checkable one.
Pretending your view never changed, when honest reflection shows that it did.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does reflection mean in Global Perspectives?
questions.modelAnswer: Reflection means thinking honestly about yourself as a learner: how you worked, what you did well or found hard, how you contributed to others, and how your views changed. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between reflection and evaluation?
questions.modelAnswer: Reflection looks inward at you and your learning; evaluation looks outward at the quality of the work, such as an argument, a source, or an outcome.

questions.prompt: A thing you are good at is a personal ______; a thing you find hard is an area for ______.
questions.modelAnswer: Strength; development (an area for development or improvement).

questions.prompt: True or false: changing your mind because of good evidence is a weakness.
questions.modelAnswer: False. Changing your mind because of good evidence is thoughtful, not weak.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between working in a team and working as a team?
questions.modelAnswer: You work in a team when you are simply placed with others; you work as a team when everyone knows their part and pulls towards one shared outcome.

questions.prompt: Name one benefit and one challenge of teamwork.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one benefit (more ideas, shared work, combined strengths, encouragement) and any one challenge (disagreement, uneven effort, talking over each other, time taken).

questions.prompt: Name one habit that helps a team overcome its challenges.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: listening carefully, being willing to compromise, making sure everyone knows their job.

questions.prompt: A ______ perspective is the view you hold after exploring different viewpoints and reasons.
Which perspective is shown in a country's laws, policies and leaders' speeches: personal, national, or global?
What does each letter of a SMART target stand for?
Rewrite this weak target to make it stronger: 'I will be better at teamwork.'
questions.modelAnswer: Any specific, checkable version, such as: in my next teacher session, I will ask each team member for one idea before I start writing.

questions.prompt: When you state your personal perspective, what short phrase should follow it to give a reason?
questions.modelAnswer: 'because ...' (as in 'I think this, because ...'), giving a reason for your view.

selfAssessment.statement: I can explain the difference between reflection and evaluation.
I can identify and explain my personal strengths.
I can identify my areas for development and say how I will improve.
I can explain my personal contribution to teamwork.
I can explain some benefits and challenges of teamwork.
I can name the skills I used or improved and link them to my strengths.
I can set clear, SMART targets for improvement.
I can explain how and why my personal perspective changed, with evidence.
I can tell a personal, a national and a global perspective apart.
I can reflect honestly on how I learn best.
